title: Telemetry-driven latency forensics: SKU comparison A100/H100/L40S
content:
Purpose:
This is a working note capturing a telemetry-driven approach we used to compare tail/mid/median latency behavior across A100, H100 and L40S cloud SKUs while varying driver and CUDA stacks. Goal: identify instrumentation blind spots that hide causal chains for P99 spikes and give actional mitigations (config knobs, sampling cadence, microbench fixes).

Context / motivation:
- Many of our previous SKU studies show different tail characteristics but the root cause attribution is noisy (driver-level interrupts, nvlink throttles, kernel-launch amplification).
- Hypothesis: telemetry sampling cadence and which counters we rely on (SM busy, memcpy stalls, kernel-queue-depth) materially change our interpretation of where latency is coming from.
- We ran small, targeted experiments that deliberately amplify specific subsystems (e.g., sustained decode to stress NVLink/HBM refresh patterns, rapid small-batch prefill to exercise kernel launch fanout).

Experiment summary (short):
- SKUs: cloud A (A100), cloud B (H100), cloud C (L40S) — representative instance families chosen for cost/availability parity; workloads pinned to single GPU.
- Runtime: serving-runtime@commit 8f3a2b4 (local perf branch).
- Models: 7B causal decoder, 8k context prefill scenario, token-by-token decode (streaming).
- Workload: steady arrival 25 qps with Poisson bursts (burst factor 3) and a contrived microburst test (20 concurrent small requests).
- CUDA tested: 11.8, 12.1, 12.2; drivers tested: 520.xx, 535.xx, 540-preview (where available).
- Telemetry collected: per-request timeline (timestamps for prefill, kv-warm, decode start/end), nvlink counters, SM util, pci-e link state events (where cloud exposes), kernel launch timestamps from eBPF on host, and GPU-side perf counters sampled via CUPTI at 200Hz and 1kHz.

Key reproducible commands (notes):
- Harness runner: ./tools/latency-harness --model small-7b --qps 25 --burst 3 --duration 15m --trace-pids --cup-ti-sample-rate 200
- To enable high-rate CUPTI sampling: export CUPTI_SAMPLE_RATE_HZ=1000; ./run-client ... (only for 2-minute debug runs, high overhead).
- eBPF kernel-launch probe: tools/ebpf/record-kernel-launch.sh --duration 900 --filter "redwood_agent"

Observations (what surprised us):
1) Sampling cadence flips attribution: with CUPTI @200Hz median latency contribution appears dominated by memcpy/PCIe stalls on L40S; with 1kHz sampling the same samples reveal a short-lived period (~30–200ms) of kernel launch serialization (many small kernels queued) that correlates with the P99 windows. In other words, coarse sampling hides short serialization hotspots.

2) Driver 535 on L40S introduced more frequent short-duration preemption/queue-reorder events that show up as 3–12ms blips in the kernel launch timeline. A100/H100 did not show the same frequency under identical workload.

3) H100 shows best median decode throughput and lowest SM busy jitter, but P99 is sensitive to sustained NVLink congestion during long-context prefill phases — manifested as grouped stalls in the NVLink counters and synchronous host-side memcpy stalls.

4) A100 had slightly higher per-kernel launch overhead for many tiny kernels (our small-batch prefill pattern), but was more stable under long sustained decode. The observed effect looks like ACM (allocator/cache-miss) amplification when host memory path phases coincide with kernel fanout.

Representative numbers (median / p95 / p99 in ms) — brief snapshot from one run (do not generalize):
- A100 (CUDA 11.8, driver 520): median 12 ms / p95 38 ms / p99 86 ms
- H100 (CUDA 12.1, driver 535): median 9 ms / p95 34 ms / p99 120 ms
- L40S (CUDA 12.2, driver 535): median 14 ms / p95 52 ms / p99 210 ms
Important: these numbers are from an isolated microbenchmark and are sensitive to the sampling and probe overhead; they are illustrative for patterns only.

Telemetry correlation examples (how we connected the dots):
- Example A (L40S P99 window): high P99 window aligned with a burst in 'kernel_launch_queued' events (from eBPF), a spike in host-side memcpy wait ns (traced by our userland shim), and a short NVLink retransmit counter uptick. Conclusion: kernel queuing + transient link noise caused backpressure.

- Example B (H100 P99 window): P99 events correlate with sustained NVLink utilization >85% during long prefill. We saw batching of host->device memcpy operations that caused queue serialization and occasional host CPU scheduling delays (observed on the per-request timeline).\Suggested mitigations: practical next steps
1) Instrumentation: add an adaptive sampling mode — default 200Hz with auto-boost to 1kHz when tail drift exceeds threshold. This reduces overhead while catching short blips.
2) Kernel packing: coalesce small kernels during prefill (packing multiple small ops into a single launch) to reduce launch fanout. Prototype patch in PR 4123 as a toggle.
3) Driver compatibility guardrails: add runtime warnings when driver version + SKU combos are known to show preemption noise (e.g., driver 535 + L40S). Work with infra to pin stable drivers for Dedicated pools.
4) NVLink-aware routing: for Dedicated, prefer GPUs with higher NVLink capacity for long-context workloads or enable controlled prefetch pacing so NVLink utilization doesn't saturate.
5) Telemetry export: push kernel-launch timelines to console tracing view and add an automated P99-attribution job that runs nightly and files JIRA tickets when a new root-cause class is detected.

Open questions and follow-ups:
- Is the 535-driver behavior a cloud provider packaging artifact or a broader driver change? Action: repro on a different region and raise vendor support ticket (INF-2871).
- How much overhead does CUPTI 1kHz sampling add to real production traffic? We need an A/B test on a low-volume Dedicated partition.
- Should we expose a user-configurable "kernel-packing" toggle in the API or keep it internal? Risk: changes may affect determinism and latency micro-behavior for some evaluation pipelines.

Micro checklist (to take this from notes -> action items):
- [ ] Re-run the L40S 535 stack on a different region to check reproducibility (owner: Daniel)
- [ ] Add adaptive-sampling prototype to runtime (owner: Marco)
- [ ] Draft a driver-compatibility advisory for infra team (owner: Priya)
- [ ] Add kernel-launch timeline to the Console trace UI (owner: obs-team ticket)
- [ ] Smoke test kernel-packing PR on canary Dedicated capacity (owner: Aisha)

Appendix: quick tips for interpreters of this data (notes on pitfalls)
- Do not trust median-only snapshots for tail-sensitive workloads; sampling granularity can hide microbursts that dominate P99.
- Beware of attributing tail latency purely to "SM busy" counters — often host-side queuing or nvlink retries are the real culprit.
- eBPF kernel-launch probes are low-noise but can miss work if filters are too coarse; correlate with per-request timestamps.

Notes to self / loose thoughts:
- Consider a nightly regression job that runs a small prefill+decode harness across all SKUs/driver combos and produces a diffs-report (delta P99 and top attribution).
- Communicate to Solutions Engineering that certain customer long-context workloads should recommend H100 Dedicated or L40S only with driver-compat checks.

End of doc (working draft).
